content: Mothers who are survivors of Ebola Virus Disease (EVD) should be supported to maintain their breast milk production. They should be encouraged to resume breastfeeding only after two consecutive milk samples test negative for the virus. Psychosocial support should also be provided to the mother and her family as needed. To facilitate the resumption of breastfeeding, mothers should be educated and supported to express breast milk regularly, either manually or using a breast pump, while adhering to EVD infection prevention and control (IPC) guidelines to minimize the risk of virus transmission. Infants who were breastfed by mothers with RT-PCR-positive breast milk should be closely monitored as high-risk contacts for 21 days from the last day of breastfeeding with the positive milk. Health workers handling potentially infectious specimens, such as breast milk or semen from EVD survivors, must wear full EVD personal protective equipment (PPE). This includes head covers, face masks, goggles or face shields, boots, coveralls or gowns, aprons, and double gloves (with outer gloves extending to the elbow for deliveries). Proper waste, sharps, and linen management, as well as strict adherence to environmental cleaning and decontamination protocols for reusable medical equipment, are essential. All waste potentially infected with the Ebola virus should be collected in designated containers and leak-proof bags, stored safely away from children and animals, and incinerated on-site whenever possible. If incineration is not feasible, burning and/or burying the waste followed by covering it with soil is recommended. Survivors should be informed that handling contaminated materials with chlorine solutions may damage the materials. Used condoms should be safely disposed of by burning, burial, or placement in pit latrines. Ebola virus may persist in certain body sites, such as the eye, male genitourinary tract, brain, spinal cord, mammary glands, and reproductive tissues, for a year or more. Elective surgeries involving these sites in EVD survivors should only be performed after careful risk-benefit analysis for both the patient and the healthcare team. In most cases, elective surgeries should be delayed for at least one year after the resolution of acute EVD. If surgery is deemed essential, it must be conducted under full EVD IPC precautions, and swabs from the implicated body site or fluid should be tested for the virus post-operatively. Risk communication is a critical component of clinical care for EVD survivors. It involves the exchange of information and concerns between healthcare providers and survivors. Effective risk communication builds trust, improves compliance with treatment, and enhances health outcomes. Survivors and their families often face stigma, fear, and misinformation, which must be addressed empathetically. Healthcare providers should use clear, jargon-free language, visual aids, and culturally appropriate communication methods. Engaging trusted community leaders and obtaining feedback from survivors can further improve communication efforts. Ultimately, effective risk communication fosters trust in healthcare services, encourages survivors to seek care, and helps prevent further transmission of the virus.
